learn.hook: In some villages, no one cuts a single branch in the forest patch near the temple. The trees are protected because the land is sacred!
points: Across India, people see certain rivers, mountains, forests, trees and lakes as sacred. This web of sacred places is called sacred geography.
Rivers such as the Ganga, Yamuna, Narmada, Godavari and Kaveri are honoured as sacred. Some devotees walk the Narmada parikramā, a long journey along both banks of the river.
Mountains like Kailash in Tibet are sacred to many traditions, including Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

Sacred groves are patches of forest protected by local communities because they are linked to a deity. They have different names: devrai in Maharashtra, kāvu in Kerala, sarnā in Jharkhand and orans in Rajasthan.
Trees like the peepal and banyan and plants like tulsi are respected in many homes. Treating nature as sacred has often helped protect it.

example.q: A sacred grove in Maharashtra has very old trees and rare plants that have disappeared from the land around it. Why?
steps: The local community believes the grove belongs to a deity.
By tradition, people do not cut trees or hunt there.
So plants and animals in the grove have been protected for a very long time.
example.answer: Because the community's belief that the grove is sacred has protected it from cutting and hunting.

learn.reallife: Many schools and nature clubs now study sacred groves, because they are like small natural museums of plants and animals.

games.title: True or false: sacred geography
items: Mount Kailash is sacred to more than one tradition.
Hindus, Buddhists and Jains, among others, revere it.
Sacred groves are protected by local communities.
By tradition people avoid cutting trees there.
The Narmada parikramā is a journey along both banks of the Narmada.
Pilgrims walk along the river on one bank and return along the other.
Only rivers can be sacred in India.
Mountains, forests, trees, lakes and towns can also be sacred.
Treating nature as sacred has helped protect many forests.
Sacred groves are a good example.

quiz.q: What is meant by 'sacred geography'?
options: A network of places in the land that people regard as holy
quiz.explain: Sacred geography is how people see rivers, mountains, forests and towns as holy and connected.
quiz.mistake: Thinks geography is only about physical features

quiz.q: A protected patch of forest linked to a local deity is called a:
quiz.explain: Sacred groves are forest patches that communities protect because they are sacred.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term

quiz.q: In Kerala, sacred groves are called:
quiz.explain: Kāvu is the Kerala name; devrai is the Maharashtra name.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up regional names

quiz.q: Which mountain is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Jains?
quiz.explain: Mount Kailash in Tibet is revered by several traditions.
quiz.mistake: Does not know that Kailash is shared

quiz.q: The Narmada parikramā is:
options: A pilgrimage walking along both banks of the Narmada
quiz.explain: Pilgrims walk along one bank to the sea and return along the other.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without knowing what parikramā means

quiz.q: How have sacred groves helped nature?
options: They are fenced by the army
People do not cut trees or hunt there by tradition
quiz.explain: Belief and tradition protect plants and animals in sacred groves.
quiz.mistake: Does not link belief with conservation

quiz.q: Which of these trees is widely respected as sacred in India?
quiz.explain: The peepal is honoured in many Indian traditions; the Buddha attained enlightenment under one at Bodh Gaya.
quiz.mistake: Picks a tree planted mainly for timber or industry

quiz.q: Sacred groves called 'orans' are found in:
quiz.explain: Orans are community-protected sacred lands in Rajasthan.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up regional names of sacred groves

teach.ask: Gappu lives in a tree. He wants to know why some trees and forests in India are called sacred.
teach.praise: Rivers, mountains and sacred groves! And being sacred keeps my forest home safe!
teach.nudge: Nice! But how does calling a forest sacred help to protect it?

learn.hook: Every year, lakhs of warkaris walk for days, singing, to Pandharpur in Maharashtra. A pilgrimage can be a journey of joy!
points: A tīrtha is a sacred place of pilgrimage. The word originally meant a ford, a place to cross a river.
The Char Dhām are Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south). By tradition they are linked with Ādi Shaṅkarāchārya, and together they connect all corners of India.
The twelve Jyotirliṅgas, sacred to devotees of Shiva, are spread across India, from Somnath in Gujarat to Rameswaram in Tamil Nadu and Kedarnath in Uttarakhand.
The Kumbh Melā is held by turn at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik; each place hosts it about once every 12 years. UNESCO lists it as an intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
In the Pandharpur Wārī, warkaris walk with the pālkhīs (palanquins) of saints Dnyāneshwar and Tukārām to the Vitthala temple at Pandharpur.

example.q: A family from Kashi (Varanasi) takes Ganga water on a pilgrimage to Rameswaram in the far south. What does this tradition show?
steps: Kashi is in the north, Rameswaram in the far south.
Carrying water from one sacred place to another links them.
Such journeys connected people from different regions, languages and foods.
example.answer: That pilgrimages tied distant parts of India together into one sacred landscape.

learn.reallife: During a yatra, pilgrims meet people from many states, try new foods and hear new languages: travel itself becomes learning.

quiz.q: The word 'tīrtha' originally meant:
options: A ford or crossing place on a river
quiz.explain: A tīrtha was a crossing place; it came to mean a sacred place of pilgrimage.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the original meaning

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the Char Dhām?
quiz.explain: The Char Dhām are Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram.
quiz.mistake: Picks a well-known tourist city

quiz.q: Which Char Dhām lies in the west of India?
quiz.explain: Dwarka is on the coast of Gujarat in the west.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up directions of the Char Dhām

quiz.q: How many Jyotirliṅgas are there in the well-known tradition?
quiz.explain: There are twelve Jyotirliṅgas spread across India.
quiz.mistake: Confuses them with the four Char Dhām

quiz.q: Which city is NOT a site of the Kumbh Melā?
quiz.explain: The four Kumbh sites are Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the four Kumbh Melā sites

quiz.q: About how often is the Kumbh Melā held at the same site?
quiz.explain: Each of the four places hosts the Kumbh roughly once every 12 years.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is an annual fair

quiz.q: The Pandharpur Wārī ends at the temple of:
quiz.explain: Warkaris walk to the Vitthala (Vithoba) temple at Pandharpur in Maharashtra.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up famous temples of different states

quiz.q: How did pilgrimages help unite India?
options: They made everyone speak one language
People from different regions travelled and met at shared sacred places
quiz.explain: Long journeys brought together people of many languages, foods and customs.
quiz.mistake: Does not see pilgrimage as a link between regions

teach.ask: Gappu asks: what is a pilgrimage, and what are some famous pilgrimages in India?
teach.praise: A sacred journey that links north, south, east and west. India is one big pilgrimage map!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you name a few famous pilgrimages, like the four dhāms or the Kumbh?

learn.hook: A Buddhist monk at Bodh Gaya, a Jain family climbing Palitana's steps, and Sikh pilgrims at the Golden Temple: India's sacred map belongs to everyone.
points: Buddhist pilgrims visit four main places linked with the Buddha's life: Lumbini (birth, in Nepal), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (passing away).
Jain pilgrims climb the Shatruñjaya hills at Palitana in Gujarat and visit Sammed Shikhar in Jharkhand. Shravanabelagola in Karnataka has the great statue of Bāhubali (Gommateshwara).
The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara of the Sikhs; its langar serves free meals to all visitors.
Sufi shrines (dargāhs), such as the dargāh of Khwāja Moinuddin Chishtī at Ajmer, are visited by people of many faiths.
Christian pilgrims visit places like the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa and the Basilica at Velankanni in Tamil Nadu. Visiting each other's sacred places shows India's spirit of respect and sharing.

example.q: Why do people of different faiths often visit the same shrine, such as the dargāh at Ajmer?
steps: Many people visit to pray for wishes, peace or thanks.
The shrine welcomes everyone, whatever their faith.
This sharing builds respect and friendship between communities.
example.answer: Because such shrines are open to all, and people of many faiths share a respect for them.

learn.reallife: When you eat at a gurdwara langar, you sit on the floor with everyone, rich or poor, of any faith: a simple lesson in equality.

games.title: Places in the Buddha's life
games.prompt: In the order of events in his life

quiz.q: Where did the Buddha attain enlightenment?
quiz.explain: The Buddha attained enlightenment under a peepal tree, the Bodhi tree, at Bodh Gaya in Bihar.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the four Buddhist sites

quiz.q: The Buddha gave his first sermon at:
quiz.explain: His first teaching was given at Sarnath near Varanasi.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the place of enlightenment with the first sermon

quiz.q: Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, is in present-day:
quiz.explain: Lumbini is in southern Nepal, close to the Indian border.
quiz.mistake: Assumes all Buddhist sites are in India

quiz.q: The Shatruñjaya hills at Palitana are sacred to:
quiz.explain: Palitana in Gujarat has hundreds of Jain temples on its hills.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the sacred places of different faiths

quiz.q: The great statue of Bāhubali (Gommateshwara) is at:
quiz.explain: The statue stands on a hill at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.
quiz.mistake: Does not know this Jain site

quiz.q: What is the langar at the Golden Temple?
options: A free community kitchen serving meals to all
quiz.explain: Everyone is welcome to eat together, whatever their background.
quiz.mistake: Does not know about the langar tradition

quiz.q: The dargāh of Khwāja Moinuddin Chishtī is in:
quiz.explain: This famous Sufi shrine is in Ajmer, Rajasthan.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up places of different faiths

quiz.q: What does the sharing of sacred places by people of different faiths show?
options: A spirit of respect and coexistence
quiz.explain: Visiting shrines of other faiths reflects India's long tradition of mutual respect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks different faiths cannot share spaces

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know which sacred places people of different faiths visit. Tell him about a few.
teach.praise: Bodh Gaya, Palitana, Amritsar, Ajmer, Goa... So many faiths, one welcoming land!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you add a sacred place of another faith, like the Sikhs or Jains?
